abbazia-greca-di-san-nilo.name: Greek Abbey of San Nilo
abbazia-greca-di-san-nilo.description: Italo-Byzantine Greek Catholic monastery in Grottaferrata, founded in 1004 by the Calabrian monk Nilus of Rossano and consecrated in 1024 by Pope John XIX; it is the last surviving Byzantine-rite Basilian monastery in Italy still in communion with Rome. The Romanesque abbey church, fronted by a 12th-13th-century mosaic of the Deesis, encloses a chapel crypt of the 5th-6th century and stands within fortifications begun under Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, and its library holds hundreds of Greek and Latin manuscripts alongside a noted book-restoration workshop.

abbazia-di-casamari.name: Abbey of Casamari
abbazia-di-casamari.description: Cistercian abbey near Veroli, built between 1203 and 1217 on the site of a Benedictine community established around 1005 amid the ruins of the Roman town of Cereatae; its monks adopted the Cistercian reform between 1140 and 1152. Regarded as one of the finest examples of Cistercian Gothic architecture in Italy, it has a three-nave basilica, a chapter house of nine vaulted bays supported by four pillars, and an extensive library.

abbazia-di-fossanova.name: Abbey of Fossanova
abbazia-di-fossanova.description: Cistercian abbey in Priverno, granted in 1134 to Burgundian monks following the reform of Bernard of Clairvaux and built between the 1160s and 1208, when Pope Innocent III consecrated its altar. Its travertine church, with rose window and octagonal lantern tower, is considered the earliest example of Gothic architecture in Italy; Thomas Aquinas died in a cell of the abbey in 1274.

abbazia-di-fruttuaria.name: Abbey of Fruttuaria
abbazia-di-fruttuaria.description: Benedictine abbey in San Benigno Canavese founded in 1003 by William of Volpiano, a monk and architect active in the Cluniac reform movement across Piedmont and France. Its Romanesque bell tower and floor mosaics with geometric and animal motifs survive from around 1100, while the church itself was rebuilt between 1770 and 1776 in a Baroque-Neoclassical style, to designs credited to Vittone and Quarini, after the medieval building was demolished.

abbazia-di-pomposa-e-museo-pomposiano.name: Abbey of Pomposa and Pomposa Museum
abbazia-di-pomposa-e-museo-pomposiano.description: Benedictine abbey near Codigoro, first documented in 874, with its Romanesque basilica consecrated in 1026 and a 48-metre bell tower completed in 1063 by the architect Deusdedit. The monk Guido d'Arezzo developed the basis of modern musical notation here in the early 11th century; the basilica preserves 14th-century Bolognese-school frescoes and an opus sectile marble floor, while the adjoining Museo Pomposiano, in the former monks' dormitory, displays marble fragments, ceramics, and liturgical objects from the complex.

abbazia-di-san-clemente-a-casauria.name: Abbey of San Clemente a Casauria
abbazia-di-san-clemente-a-casauria.description: Benedictine abbey near Castiglione a Casauria, founded in 871 by Emperor Louis II as a votive offering and dedicated to Pope Clement I, whose relics it received the following year, making it a major pilgrimage site. Its Romanesque-Gothic facade, completed under Abbot Leonate between 1156 and 1182, has a bronze door of 72 panels and sculpted portals narrating the abbey's foundation, above a crypt of nine naves built with reused Roman materials.

abbazia-di-santo-spirito-al-morrone.name: Abbey of Santo Spirito al Morrone
abbazia-di-santo-spirito-al-morrone.description: Celestine abbey on the slopes of Monte Morrone near Sulmona, founded in the mid-13th century by the hermit Pietro da Morrone, later Pope Celestine V, and consecrated in the late 1260s; it became the motherhouse of the Celestine congregation in 1293. Rebuilt with a Baroque church around 1730 after earthquake damage, it retains a medieval crypt and 15th-century frescoes by Giovanni da Sulmona, and served as a prison from 1868 until 1993.

abbazia-di-vezzolano.name: Abbey of Vezzolano
abbazia-di-vezzolano.description: Romanesque-Gothic canonry near Albugnano, first documented in 1095 and largely built between the mid-12th and early 13th centuries, traditionally, though legendarily, linked to a foundation by Charlemagne. Its facade in alternating bands of sandstone and brick and its sculpted rood screen of 1189, depicting the Dormition of the Virgin and the genealogy of Christ, make it one of Piedmont's most significant Romanesque monuments, despite never having formally held abbey status.

anfiteatro-campano.name: Amphitheatre of Capua
anfiteatro-campano.description: Roman amphitheatre in Santa Maria Capua Vetere, ancient Capua, built around 100 CE (construction date debated among scholars), restored under Hadrian in 119 and inaugurated by Antoninus Pius in 155. With an estimated capacity of around 60,000 and a four-storey elliptical facade rising 46 metres, it is the second-largest surviving Roman amphitheatre after the Colosseum, which it is thought to have influenced; it was also home to a renowned gladiator school, and in 2024 it was included in the UNESCO World Heritage listing for ancient Capua.

anfiteatro-verlasce.name: Verlasce Amphitheatre
anfiteatro-verlasce.description: Roman amphitheatre in Venafro, Molise, known locally as the Verlasce, preserving the remains of the ancient town's arena and spectacle building.

antiquarium-e-area-archeologica-di-lucus.name: Antiquarium and Archaeological Area of Lucus Feroniae
antiquarium-e-area-archeologica-di-lucus.description: Etruscan and Roman site near Capena, developed around a sanctuary of the Italic goddess Feronia that was plundered by Hannibal in 211 BCE and later refounded as the Roman colony of Lucus Feroniae under Julius Caesar and Augustus. The archaeological area preserves a forum with temples, houses, a Trajanic-era amphitheatre, baths, and the large Villa of the Volusii Saturnini, while the antiquarium displays statuary, jewellery, inscriptions, and reliefs recovered from the site.

antiquarium-statale-di-numana.name: State Antiquarium of Numana
antiquarium-statale-di-numana.description: Archaeological museum in Numana, opened in 1974, devoted to finds from the Picene necropolises of Numana and Sirolo, one of the principal centres of Picene civilization in the pre-Roman Iron Age. Its collection includes bronze and terracotta grave goods, the remains of two chariots, and material from the richly furnished 'Tomb of the Queen' at the nearby I Pini necropolis, alongside evidence of the later Roman settlement.

arco-di-malborghetto.name: Arch of Malborghetto
arco-di-malborghetto.description: Roman monumental arch on the Via Flaminia north of Rome, originally a four-way tetrapylon built in the early 4th century, possibly marking the site of Constantine's camp before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312. Converted into a Greek-cross church around the 11th century by walling up its arches and adding an apse, it now houses a small archaeological museum.

area-archeologica-villa-romana-di-torre.name: Archaeological Area of the Roman Villa of Torre
area-archeologica-villa-romana-di-torre.description: Archaeological area of a Roman villa within Torre Castle park on the Noncello river at Pordenone, occupied between the 1st century BC and the 4th century AD and combining residential and productive quarters, including a thermal bath complex. First excavated between 1950 and 1952 by Count Giuseppe di Ragogna and further investigated and restored by the Superintendency in the 1980s and 1990s, it is one of the most significant Roman-era sites in Friuli.

area-archeologica-antica-citta-di-ferent.name: Archaeological Area of the Ancient City of Ferento
area-archeologica-antica-citta-di-ferent.description: Ruins of Ferentium, an Etruscan and later Roman town near Viterbo that flourished as a municipium in the early imperial period and was the birthplace of Emperor Otho, before being destroyed by nearby Viterbo in 1172. The site preserves a well-excavated Roman theatre still used for summer performances, along with the remains of a forum, baths, and an amphitheatre.

area-archeologica-del-tempio-italico-di-.name: Archaeological Area of the Italic Temple of Casalbore
area-archeologica-del-tempio-italico-di-.description: Samnite sanctuary near Casalbore, in the Macchia Porcara area, dating to the 3rd century BCE and possibly dedicated to the goddess Mefitis, one of the notable religious sites of ancient Irpinia. Tombs found nearby date back as far as the 6th century BCE, pointing to a much longer history of funerary and cultic use at the location.

area-archeologica-della-citta-romana-di-.name: Archaeological Area of the Roman City of Industria
area-archeologica-della-citta-romana-di-.description: Archaeological area of the Roman town of Industria, known in pre-Roman times as Bodincomagus, an active river port and commercial centre on the Po between the 1st century BC and the 5th century AD. Excavations at the San Giovanni locality have brought to light the forum, a temple dedicated to Isis, stretches of the town walls and shops, before the settlement was destroyed by fire following a Hunnic raid.

area-archeologica-di-augusta-bagiennorum.name: Archaeological Area of Augusta Bagiennorum
area-archeologica-di-augusta-bagiennorum.description: Roman town founded around the turn of the 1st century CE near modern Bene Vagienna, Piedmont, named after the Ligurian Bagienni. Excavated since 1896, the site preserves a forum with porticoed shops, a three-nave basilica, a theatre with quadriporticus, an amphitheatre and a paleochristian basilica of the 5th-6th centuries built over a temple.

area-archeologica-di-carsulae.name: Archaeological Area of Carsulae
area-archeologica-di-carsulae.description: Archaeological area of Carsulae, a Roman town that grew up along the Via Flaminia, laid out by the censor Gaius Flaminius around 220 BC, and developed into a full municipium during the Augustan age. Visible remains include the paved road with its cart ruts, the forum with twin temples, a theatre and amphitheatre, the three-arched Arch of San Damiano, a basilica and baths; the town was gradually abandoned after an earthquake in the 5th-6th century.

area-archeologica-di-comeana-tumuli-di-m.name: Comeana Archaeological Area - Montefortini and Boschetti Tumuli
area-archeologica-di-comeana-tumuli-di-m.description: Etruscan necropolis at Comeana, near Carmignano in Tuscany, grouping the Montefortini and Boschetti tumuli. The Montefortini mound, an artificial hill 70 metres across discovered in 1965, contains a chamber tomb of the Orientalizing period (c. 625-575 BCE) and a later tholos tomb, which yielded bucchero ware, ivory, amber and Egyptian glass now in the Artimino Archaeological Museum.

area-archeologica-di-conza.name: Archaeological Area of Conza
area-archeologica-di-conza.description: Archaeological area of ancient Compsa, chief town of the Hirpini Samnites before becoming a Roman municipium; Julius Caesar mentions it in his account of the civil war of 48 BC. Remains brought to light after the 1980 earthquake include the forum, an amphitheatre, baths, houses predating the 2nd century BC and inscriptions, now displayed in an on-site antiquarium.

area-archeologica-di-feltre.name: Archaeological Area of Feltre
area-archeologica-di-feltre.description: Underground archaeological area beneath the historic centre of Feltre, revealing structures from the Roman era to the early medieval period, including the presumed seat of a professional association (schola). Nearby, the Baptistery preserves Roman-era passages and the Cathedral crypt retains traces of a Roman mosaic floor; the site is visited on guided tours run by the local heritage association Il Fondaco per Feltre.

area-archeologica-di-libarna.name: Archaeological Area of Libarna
area-archeologica-di-libarna.description: Archaeological area of Libarna, a town of the Ligurian Dectunini that came under Roman control in 191 BC and grew after the opening of the Via Postumia in 148 BC, reaching its peak as a colony in the 1st century AD before being abandoned in 452 following barbarian invasions. Excavations begun in 1820 have uncovered a 60x65-metre amphitheatre, a theatre, the forum with its porticoes, baths and residential quarters, with major finds such as mosaics and bronzes now held in Turin's Museum of Antiquities.

area-archeologica-di-nervia.name: Archaeological Area of Nervia
area-archeologica-di-nervia.description: Archaeological area of Albintimilium, capital of the ancient Ligurian Intemelii and later a Roman municipium from 89 BC, laid out on a grid plan along the Via Julia Augusta. Excavations conducted from the late 19th century onward, notably by Girolamo Rossi and Nino Lamboglia, have revealed a theatre, baths with the mosaic known as the Arion Mosaic, residential blocks and a necropolis of around 185 tombs.

area-archeologica-di-volsini.name: Archaeological Area of Volsinii
area-archeologica-di-volsini.description: Site of Volsinii Novi, the Roman city founded on the shore of Lake Bolsena after the Etruscan capital Volsinii (modern Orvieto) was destroyed by the consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus in 264 BCE. Excavated from 1946 to 1986, the area preserves the Roman street grid, forum and an Augustan-era basilica, while temple remains at the nearby Campo della Fiera have been identified with the federal Etruscan sanctuary of Fanum Voltumnae.

area-archeologica-e-antiquarium-di-velei.name: Archaeological Area and Antiquarium of Veleia
area-archeologica-e-antiquarium-di-velei.description: Archaeological area and antiquarium of Veleia, a settlement of the Ligurian Veleiates that became a Roman municipium in 49 BC and prospered thanks to its thermal springs despite lying off the main trade routes. Rediscovered in 1747 with the finding of the bronze Tabula Alimentaria Traianea, a record of welfare loans granted by Trajan, the site has been excavated since 1760 to reveal the forum, a basilica, houses, a theatre and baths, with finds displayed in the on-site antiquarium.

basilica-di-san-francesco-viterbo.name: Basilica of San Francesco alla Rocca
basilica-di-san-francesco-viterbo.description: Franciscan basilica in Viterbo begun in 1237 on land donated by Pope Gregory IX, with a Romanesque facade and a Gothic interior on a Latin-cross plan. It holds the tombs of two 13th-century popes, Clement IV (d. 1268) by Pietro di Oderisio and Adrian V (d. 1276) attributed to Arnolfo di Cambio; severely damaged by bombing in 1944, it was raised to minor basilica status in 1949 and reopened after reconstruction in 1953.

basilica-di-san-saturnino.name: Basilica of San Saturnino
basilica-di-san-saturnino.description: The oldest church in Cagliari and dedicated to the city's patron saint, built from the 5th century over the burial site of the martyr Saturninus and first recorded between 507 and 523, when Fulgentius of Ruspe founded a monastery beside it. Originally a Greek-cross domed building blending Byzantine and early Christian forms, it was rebuilt in Provençal Romanesque style by Benedictine monks after 1089 and reconsecrated in 1119; only the central domed bay and the three-aisled east arm survive today, following restoration after World War II bombing damage.

basilica-di-sant-apollinare-in-classe.name: Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe
basilica-di-sant-apollinare-in-classe.description: Basilica built between 532 and 536 on the orders of Bishop Ursicinus and financed by the banker Julianus Argentarius, dedicated to Saint Apollinaris, Ravenna's first bishop, and consecrated in 549 by Archbishop Maximian. The three-aisled basilica, with columns of Proconnesian marble and a 9th-century cylindrical bell tower, preserves in its apse a 6th-century mosaic of the Transfiguration showing Sant'Apollinare among twelve lambs beneath a jewelled cross; it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site 'Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna', inscribed in 1996.

basilica-paleocristiana-di-via-madonna-d.name: Early Christian Basilica of Via Madonna del Mare
basilica-paleocristiana-di-via-madonna-d.description: Remains of an early Christian basilica, partially uncovered in 1963 during roadworks in Trieste, built in two phases between the early 5th and early 6th century on a Latin-cross plan with a polygonal apse. A floor inscription referring to the 'Sancta Ecclesia Tergestina' attests to its role as a place of worship for the early Christian community of ancient Tergeste.

battistero-degli-ariani.name: Arian Baptistery
battistero-degli-ariani.description: Octagonal brick baptistery commissioned by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great in the late 5th century for Ravenna's Arian community. Its dome preserves a mosaic of the Baptism of Christ surrounded by the twelve apostles offering crowns; it forms part of the UNESCO World Heritage site 'Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna', inscribed in 1996.

biblioteca-nazionale-marciana-sale-monum.name: Marciana National Library - Monumental Halls and Ridotti dei Procuratori
biblioteca-nazionale-marciana-sale-monum.description: Monumental halls of the Marciana Library in Venice, built by Jacopo Sansovino between 1537 and 1588 to house the manuscripts bequeathed by Cardinal Bessarion in 1468. The Renaissance building, praised by Palladio as one of the richest and most ornate since antiquity, has a facade modelled on Rome's Theatre of Marcellus and ceilings and walls painted by Titian, Tintoretto, Veronese and Schiavone; the library's collections moved to the adjoining Zecca in 1904, leaving the halls as a museum space.

cappella-espiatoria.name: Expiatory Chapel
cappella-espiatoria.description: Memorial chapel in Monza marking the spot where King Umberto I of Italy was assassinated by the anarchist Gaetano Bresci on 29 July 1900, commissioned by Queen Margherita and King Victor Emmanuel III and designed by Giuseppe Sacconi, architect of the Vittoriano in Rome, completed after his death by Guido Cirilli and inaugurated in 1910. The 35-metre circular structure, decorated with Byzantine-style mosaics and polychrome marble, stands over a Greek-cross crypt marking the exact site of the killing and houses a Pietà by Lodovico Pogliaghi.

cappella-dell-annunziata.name: Chapel of the Annunziata
cappella-dell-annunziata.description: Small chapel in Cori, built in the 14th century along a medieval road linking the town to the Pedemontana route, with its oratory decorated over the course of the 15th century. The interior preserves fresco cycles illustrating scenes from the Old and New Testaments alongside stories of saints and local tradition.

casa-museo-boncompagni-ludovisi.name: Boncompagni Ludovisi House Museum of Decorative Arts
casa-museo-boncompagni-ludovisi.description: House museum in the early 20th-century Villino Boncompagni Ludovisi in Rome, bequeathed to the Italian state by Princess Blanceflor de Bildt Boncompagni in 1972 and opened to the public in 1995. Its five rooms display the family's original furniture, tapestries, paintings and ceramics alongside a collection of 20th-century Italian fashion, including garments by Valentino, Fernanda Gattinoni and Roberto Capucci, enriched in 1996 by the wardrobe of art historian Palma Bucarelli.

casa-museo-hendrik-christian-andersen.name: Hendrik Christian Andersen House Museum
casa-museo-hendrik-christian-andersen.description: The former residence and studio of Norwegian-American sculptor Hendrik Christian Andersen (1872–1940), who settled in Rome and, on his death, bequeathed the building — known as Villa Hélène, on Via Pasquale Stanislao Mancini near Piazzale Flaminio — along with more than 400 of his works to the Italian state. The museum displays his monumental sculptures, paintings, and models for his unrealized project for an ideal 'World City,' developed with the architect Ernest Hébrard.

casa-museo-mario-praz.name: Mario Praz House Museum
casa-museo-mario-praz.description: The former apartment of the literary scholar Mario Praz (1896–1982), founder of the chair of English literature at Rome's Sapienza University, on the third floor of Palazzo Primoli on Via Zanardelli. The Italian state acquired his collection of more than 1,000 Neoclassical and Biedermeier decorative objects, furniture, and paintings in 1986, and the museum opened to the public in 1995 with the rooms arranged as Praz himself had kept them.

casa-pasolini.name: Pasolini House
casa-pasolini.description: The small apartment on Via Giovanni Tagliere in Rome's Rebibbia district where the writer and filmmaker Pier Paolo Pasolini lived with his mother, Susanna Colussi, from 1951 to 1954, one of his hardest periods after moving to Rome; it was here that he began his first novel, Ragazzi di vita. Donated to the state by the producer Pietro Valsecchi, the two-room flat was restored and opened to the public as a museum in 2025, on the fiftieth anniversary of Pasolini's death.

casa-di-san-tommaso-d-aquino.name: House of Saint Thomas Aquinas
casa-di-san-tommaso-d-aquino.description: A historic house preserved in the town of Aquino, in Lazio, ancestral seat of the counts of Aquino, the noble family of the medieval theologian Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), who is venerated as the town's patron saint and after whom Aquino styles itself 'the City of Saint Thomas.' The house is listed among the town's historic civil buildings, together with the surviving tower of the counts' castle, and is part of Lazio's state museum network.

castel-sant-angelo.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
castel-sant-angelo.description: Originally built as a mausoleum for the Emperor Hadrian, begun around 135 AD and completed under Antoninus Pius in 139, the monument was incorporated into Rome's Aurelian Walls as a fortress in 403 and later became a papal stronghold linked to the Vatican by a covered passage, the Passetto di Borgo. It takes its name from a vision of the Archangel Michael attributed to Pope Gregory I, and today houses a museum with Renaissance papal apartments frescoed by artists including Pinturicchio and Perin del Vaga, alongside the medieval fortifications and former prison cells.

castel-sant-elmo.name: Castel Sant'Elmo
castel-sant-elmo.description: A star-shaped fortress on Naples' Vomero hill, begun in 1329 under King Robert of Anjou on the site of a tenth-century church dedicated to Sant'Erasmo, and largely rebuilt with its distinctive six-pointed plan in the 1530s–40s under the Spanish viceroy Pedro de Toledo. Long used as a military prison — its inmates included the philosopher Tommaso Campanella — it has been open as a museum since 1988 and now houses the permanent exhibition 'Novecento a Napoli' (1910–1980) alongside temporary shows.

castel-del-monte.name: Castel del Monte
castel-del-monte.description: An octagonal fortress on the Murge plateau near Andria, built around 1240–1250 on the order of the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, who fused Islamic, classical, and northern European architectural elements in its design. Its original function remains debated, with theories ranging from hunting lodge to seat of learning, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996 for the mathematical and astronomical precision of its plan.

castello-angioino-di-copertino.name: Angevin Castle of Copertino
castello-angioino-di-copertino.description: Castle in Copertino, Puglia, whose oldest quadrangular tower dates from the 13th-14th centuries; it was rebuilt as a star-shaped Renaissance fortress with four corner bastions by the military architect Evangelista Menga, completed in 1540 for Alfonso Castriota. It features a Catalan-Durazzo portal and the chapel of San Marco, frescoed from 1557 by Gianserio Strafella, and was declared a national monument in 1886.

castello-bufalini.name: Bufalini Castle
castello-bufalini.description: A castle in San Giustino, in Umbria's upper Tiber valley, built from 1487 for Niccolò Bufalini as a square fortress with four watchtowers, designed by the Roman architect Mariano Savelli. From 1530 Giulio I Bufalini had it converted into an elegant residence with loggias by the Florentine architect Nanni Unghero, and the Bufalini brothers commissioned the Mannerist painter Cristofano Gherardi to fresco rooms including the Sala del Trono; an Italian garden was added in the late 17th century, and the state acquired the castle in 1988.

castello-piccolomini-collezione-torlonia.name: Piccolomini Castle — Torlonia Collection and Museum of Sacred Art of the Marsica
castello-piccolomini-collezione-torlonia.description: A castle in Celano, in the Marsica region of Abruzzo, first fortified in 1223 during a siege by the Emperor Frederick II and rebuilt from 1392 for Pietro II Berardi, count of Celano; after 1463 it was transformed into a refined Renaissance residence with a two-tiered arcaded courtyard for Antonio Todeschini Piccolomini, nephew of Pope Pius II. Restored after severe damage in the 1915 earthquake and declared a national monument in 1893, it now displays the Museo d'arte sacra della Marsica together with material from the collection of the Torlonia family, who acquired vast estates in the nearby Fucino basin after draining the lake in the 19th century.

castello-di-capua.name: Capua Castle
castello-di-capua.description: A medieval square fortress on the Serrone hill in Gambatesa, Molise, crowned with Guelph battlements and corner towers; it passed in the 15th century to Andrea di Capua, whose family — later dukes of Termoli, not to be confused with the city of Capua — gave the castle its name and converted it into a Renaissance palace in the 16th century, adding a rusticated portal and a loggia. In 1550 Vincenzo I di Capua commissioned the painter Donato da Copertino to fresco several rooms with landscapes, grotesques, and mythological scenes; restored, the castle is now state-owned and displays the frescoes as a picture gallery.

castello-di-civitacampomarano.name: Civitacampomarano Castle
castello-di-civitacampomarano.description: A quadrangular castle with three cylindrical corner towers in the Molise hill town of Civitacampomarano, replacing an earlier 12th-century watchtower and dating, in its present form, largely to the 13th-century Angevin period. Its eastern facade bears the coat of arms of Paolo di Sangro; the interior preserves coffered ceilings and a courtyard with the Fountain of the Fauns, and the castle, declared a national monument in 1979 and bought by the state in 1988, now serves as a museum.

castello-di-montesarchio-e-museo-archeol.name: Montesarchio Castle and National Archaeological Museum of Sannio Caudino
castello-di-montesarchio-e-museo-archeol.description: A hilltop castle above Montesarchio, in Campania's Caudine Valley, with origins traced to the 8th century and later used as a prison, whose 19th-century Bourbon wing now houses the National Archaeological Museum of Sannio Caudino. Opened in 2007, the museum displays around 300 artifacts from the ancient Samnite centers of Caudium, Saticula, and Telesia, most notably a 4th-century-BC crater by the Paestan vase-painter Assteas depicting the Rape of Europa, restituted in 2005 after having been looted and sold abroad.

castello-di-san-terenzo.name: San Terenzo Castle
castello-di-san-terenzo.description: A small pentagonal fortress overlooking the village of San Terenzo, a hamlet of Lerici on the Gulf of Poets, built from 1360 around an earlier watchtower to defend the coast against pirate raids. With its square keep and later corner towers and barbican, it worked alongside the larger Lerici castle to guard the gulf, and since 2014 it has been managed as a museum by Italy's regional museum authority.

castello-di-torrechiara.name: Torrechiara Castle
castello-di-torrechiara.description: A castle near Langhirano, in the hills above Parma, built between 1448 and 1460 for the condottiero Pier Maria II de' Rossi as both a stronghold and a residence for his companion Bianca Pellegrini, with a triple ring of walls and four towers around a central Corte d'Onore. Its Camera d'Oro is frescoed in Gothic style, attributed to Benedetto Bembo or his circle, with scenes of courtly life and portraits of the couple; since June 2024 the castle has formed part of the Pilotta Monumental Complex in Parma.

castello-svevo-di-bari.name: Swabian Castle of Bari
castello-svevo-di-bari.description: Castle built in 1132 for the Norman king Roger II on an earlier fortified site, destroyed in 1156 and rebuilt after 1233 by the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. Enlarged under Angevin and Aragonese rule, with the outer defensive wall added by Isabella of Aragon, Duchess of Bari, it now houses a museum of medieval finds from the castle excavations, a collection of plaster casts of regional monuments, and multimedia displays on the city's history.

castello-svevo-di-trani.name: Swabian Castle of Trani
castello-svevo-di-trani.description: Fortress built between 1233 and 1249 on the orders of the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, with a near-square plan and four corner towers modeled on Crusader and Roman castra design. Used as a royal residence and treasury under the Angevins, reinforced for artillery warfare under Charles V, and later a prison from 1844 to 1974, it now houses a small museum of finds recovered during its restoration.

cenacolo-vinciano.name: Leonardo's Last Supper
cenacolo-vinciano.description: Wall painting of the Last Supper executed by Leonardo da Vinci between 1494 and 1498 in the refectory of the Dominican convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, commissioned by Duke Ludovico Sforza, known as Il Moro. Painted in tempera and oil on dry plaster rather than true fresco, it deteriorated rapidly and underwent a major restoration completed in 1999; the convent has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1980.

cenacolo-di-andrea-del-sarto-a-san-salvi.name: Andrea del Sarto's Last Supper at San Salvi
cenacolo-di-andrea-del-sarto-a-san-salvi.description: Fresco of the Last Supper painted by Andrea del Sarto between 1511 and 1527 in the refectory of the former Vallombrosan monastery of San Salvi, on the outskirts of Florence. It was one of the few artworks outside the city walls to survive the 1529-1530 siege of Florence and is preserved today in a small dedicated museum.

cenacolo-di-sant-apollonia.name: Andrea del Castagno's Last Supper at Sant'Apollonia
cenacolo-di-sant-apollonia.description: Fresco of the Last Supper painted by Andrea del Castagno around 1445-1450 in the refectory of the former convent of Sant'Apollonia in Florence, with scenes of the Resurrection, Crucifixion, and Deposition on the wall above. Hidden from public view by monastic enclosure until the convent's suppression in 1866, it is now a small state museum.

certosa-di-san-giacomo-e-museo-archeolog.name: Certosa di San Giacomo and National Archaeological Museum of Capri
certosa-di-san-giacomo-e-museo-archeolog.description: The oldest monastery on Capri, built in 1371 by Count Giacomo Arcucci on land donated by Queen Joanna I of Naples for Carthusian monks, with a Renaissance-era cloister added after pirate raids. Secularised under Joachim Murat in 1808 and later used as barracks and a military prison, it has housed a museum devoted to the painter Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach since 1975, and in 2024 became home to the National Archaeological Museum of Capri, with about 120 artifacts spanning the Republican to medieval periods.

certosa-di-san-lorenzo.name: Charterhouse of San Lorenzo
certosa-di-san-lorenzo.description: Carthusian monastery founded in 1306 by Tommaso II Sanseverino, with the confirmation of King Charles II of Anjou, and expanded over the following centuries into the largest charterhouse in Italy, largely rebuilt in Baroque style between the 16th and 18th centuries around three cloisters. Suppressed in the 19th century, it has housed the Provincial Archaeological Museum of Western Lucania since 1957 and was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1998.

certosa-di-san-martino.name: Charterhouse of San Martino
certosa-di-san-martino.description: Carthusian monastery founded in 1325 by Charles, Duke of Calabria, and consecrated in 1368, largely rebuilt in Baroque style in the 17th century under the architect Cosimo Fanzago. Since 1866 it has housed the National Museum of San Martino, devoted to the art and history of Naples from the Bourbon period to Italian unification, arranged around three cloisters and hanging gardens overlooking the city.

certosa-di-trisulti.name: Charterhouse of Trisulti
certosa-di-trisulti.description: Monastic complex in the hills above Collepardo, built from 1204 near the site of an earlier Benedictine hermitage founded around 996 by Saint Dominic of Sora, and assigned to Carthusian monks whose church of San Bartolomeo was consecrated in 1211; the Cistercians have held it since 1947. It preserves a monastic pharmacy with 18th-century frescoes and a historic library, together with later Baroque additions including the 1798 church facade.

chiesa-di-san-francesco-d-assisi.name: Church of St Francis of Assisi (Gerace)
chiesa-di-san-francesco-d-assisi.description: Franciscan church in Gerace built in the early 13th century on the remains of an earlier Romanesque building, with an adjoining convent founded by Brother Daniele, a companion of Francis of Assisi; the church was completed by 1252. It preserves a Gothic portal with Arab-Norman decoration, a 17th-century polychrome marble altar, and the 1372 marble sarcophagus of the knight Nicola Ruffo.

chiesa-di-san-pietro.name: Church of St Peter (Tuscania)
chiesa-di-san-pietro.description: Romanesque church on the hill of San Pietro above Tuscania, built mainly between the 11th and 12th centuries on the site of an earlier building and serving as the town's cathedral until 1573. Its facade combines a rose window with Cosmatesque decoration of zodiac and seasonal-labor motifs, and its crypt, supported by 28 reused ancient columns, contains a 14th-century fresco of the town's patron saints.

chiesa-di-san-pietro-ad-alba-fucens.name: Church of San Pietro ad Alba Fucens
chiesa-di-san-pietro-ad-alba-fucens.description: Church overlooking the Roman archaeological site of Alba Fucens in Massa d'Albe, Abruzzo, built over a temple of Apollo and rebuilt with three naves in the early 12th century by Benedictine monks, whose possession of the site was confirmed by Emperor Louis the Pious in 866. It preserves a Cosmatesque ambo and a 1215 iconostasis with twisted columns and porphyry inlay; largely destroyed by the 1915 Avezzano earthquake, it was rebuilt in a near-total anastylosis by Raffaello Delogu between 1955 and 1957.

chiesa-di-san-pietro-ad-oratorium.name: Church of San Pietro ad Oratorium
chiesa-di-san-pietro-ad-oratorium.description: Romanesque abbey church near Capestrano, in Abruzzo, traditionally said to have been founded in the 8th century by the Lombard king Desiderius and rebuilt between the late 11th and early 12th centuries; it was consecrated around 1100 by Pope Paschal II, who brought relics of Saint Peter for the occasion. It preserves apse frescoes of Christ with the evangelists and the Elders of the Apocalypse, and a carved Sator-square palindrome on its facade.

chiesa-di-santa-maria-maggiore-di-tuscan.name: Church of Santa Maria Maggiore (Tuscania)
chiesa-di-santa-maria-maggiore-di-tuscan.description: Romanesque church in Tuscania, first documented in 852 and consecrated in 1206, built on a three-nave basilica plan with a semicircular apse. Its facade has three portals, including a splayed central portal flanked by spiral columns carved with figures of the apostles and a rose window with symbols of the evangelists, while the interior preserves a 13th-century apse fresco of the Twelve Apostles and a 14th-century Last Judgment attributed to Gregorio and Donato d'Arezzo.

compendio-garibaldino-di-caprera.name: Garibaldi's House and Estate, Caprera
compendio-garibaldino-di-caprera.description: Historic estate on the island of Caprera, near La Maddalena in Sardinia, where Giuseppe Garibaldi settled permanently from 1856 and built his home, the Casa Bianca, later enlarged in 1861 and 1880; he died there on 2 June 1882 and is buried in the family cemetery on the grounds. Occupied by his descendants until 1959, the estate opened as a museum in 1978 and preserves the house with its original furnishings, alongside farm buildings and personal memorabilia.

complesso-monumentale-e-museo-della-cert.name: Monumental Complex and Museum of the Certosa di Pavia
complesso-monumentale-e-museo-della-cert.description: Museum in the Palazzo Ducale of the Certosa di Pavia, the Carthusian monastery that served as a summer residence for the Visconti and Sforza dukes of Milan, its facade redesigned in 1625 by Francesco Maria Richini. Founded as an institution in 1892 and opened to the public in 1911 under the architect Luca Beltrami, who modelled it on Paris's Trocadéro, it displays over 200 plaster casts, sculptures by Giovanni Antonio Amadeo and Agostino Busti ('il Bambaia'), and paintings by Bramantino, Bernardino Luini and Vincenzo Campi.

complesso-monumentale-della-certosa-di-c.name: Monumental Complex of the Certosa di Calci
complesso-monumentale-della-certosa-di-c.description: Carthusian monastery in the Val Graziosa near Calci, Tuscany, founded on 30 May 1366 by Archbishop Francesco Moricotti of Pisa and inhabited by monks until 1970. Rebuilt in Baroque style through the 18th century, with a church front marked by a double-ramp staircase, its western wing has housed the University of Pisa's Natural History Museum since 1981, including one of Europe's largest cetacean galleries and Italy's largest freshwater aquarium.

complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta.name: Pilotta Palace Monumental Complex
complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta.description: Vast Farnese palace complex built from 1580 in Parma's historic centre, taking its name from the Basque pelota game Spanish soldiers once played in its courtyard. Left unfinished when construction halted in 1611, it now houses the Teatro Farnese, the National Gallery, the Palatina Library and the National Archaeological Museum under one roof.

complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-bibl.name: Pilotta Palace Monumental Complex - Palatina Library
complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-bibl.description: Library within the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma, founded in 1761 by dukes Filippo and Ferdinando di Borbone and formally inaugurated in 1769. It holds some 700,000 items, including manuscripts, incunabula, prints and drawings, among them one of the largest collections of Hebrew manuscripts held by any public library.

complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-gall.name: Pilotta Palace Monumental Complex - National Gallery of Parma
complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-gall.description: Art museum within the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma, established in 1760 by Duke Filippo I di Borbone around paintings kept from the Farnese collection after most of it was moved to Naples in 1734. Its holdings span the Renaissance to the eighteenth century, including works by Correggio and Parmigianino, Leonardo da Vinci's La Scapigliata, and paintings by Tiepolo, Canaletto and Guercino.

complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-muse.name: Pilotta Palace Monumental Complex - Bodoni Museum
complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-muse.description: Museum within the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma dedicated to the printer and type designer Giambattista Bodoni (1740-1813), officially established in 1963 and moved in 2022 to a ground-floor space within the Palatina Library. It preserves thousands of volumes, letters and typographic tools from his workshop, along with a reconstruction of his printing press.

complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-muse.name: Pilotta Palace Monumental Complex - National Archaeological Museum of Parma
complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-muse.description: Founded in 1760 by Duke Filippo di Borbone after the discovery of Roman bronzes at Velleia, one of the earliest archaeological museums in Italy. Its holdings span twelve Julio-Claudian marble statues and the Tabula Alimentaria from Velleia, an Egyptian section built up under Maria Luigia, and prehistoric finds from the Terramare culture.

complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-teat.name: Pilotta Palace Monumental Complex - Farnese Theatre
complesso-monumentale-della-pilotta-teat.description: Wooden court theatre within the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma, built from 1618 for Duke Ranuccio I Farnese to a design by Giovan Battista Aleotti and inaugurated in 1628. Constructed of fir and stucco painted to imitate marble, it seated about 3,000 spectators and is considered one of the earliest theatres with a permanent proscenium arch.

complesso-monumentale-di-san-vincenzo-al.name: Monumental Complex of San Vincenzo al Volturno
complesso-monumentale-di-san-vincenzo-al.description: Benedictine abbey founded around 731 by three Beneventan noblemen, which grew into one of the great monastic centres of early medieval Italy before being sacked by Saracen raiders in 881. Excavations have uncovered the vast ninth-century basilica of San Vincenzo Maggiore and the crypt of Epyphanius, decorated with Carolingian-era frescoes.

complesso-monumentale-e-biblioteca-dei-g.name: Girolamini Monumental Complex and Library of Naples
complesso-monumentale-e-biblioteca-dei-g.description: Oratorian convent complex in Naples's historic centre, whose library opened to the public in 1586 and is the oldest in the city and second-oldest in Italy. Redesigned in the eighteenth century by Arcangelo Guglielmelli, it holds around 160,000 volumes, including incunabula and Giambattista Vico's personal collection, and reopened in 2022 after a lengthy restoration following a 2012 theft scandal.

concordia-sagittaria-area-archeologica-s.name: Concordia Sagittaria, Archaeological Area beneath the Cathedral
concordia-sagittaria-area-archeologica-s.description: Archaeological site beneath the cathedral of Concordia Sagittaria, near Venice, uncovering the foundations of an early Christian basilica within the Roman city of Iulia Concordia, founded around 42 BCE at the crossing of the Via Annia and Via Postumia. Nearby excavations have also revealed Roman warehouses, baths, a bridge and a soldiers' burial ground.

crypta-neapolitana.name: Crypta Neapolitana
crypta-neapolitana.description: Roman road tunnel cut through the Posillipo hill between Naples and Pozzuoli, likely excavated under Augustus to shorten the route along the coast. Its entrance stands beside the site traditionally identified as Virgil's tomb, which drew pilgrims and Grand Tour travellers for centuries.

direzione-regionale-musei-nazionali-sard.name: Regional Directorate of National Museums of Sardinia
direzione-regionale-musei-nazionali-sard.description: Administrative office in Sassari overseeing Italy's state-run museums and monuments in Sardinia, part of the Ministry of Culture's system of regional museum directorates.

drugstore-museum-e-circuito-necropoli-po.name: Drugstore Museum and Portuense Necropolis Circuit
drugstore-museum-e-circuito-necropoli-po.description: Small museum and visitor circuit in Rome connected to the ancient Roman necropolis of Portuense, along the historic road that led to the port of Portus.

fondi-ex-pasqualis.name: Fondi ex Pasqualis
fondi-ex-pasqualis.description: Archaeological excavation area in Aquileia, one of the largest Roman cities in northern Italy and a UNESCO World Heritage site, managed by the Aquileia Foundation. The site preserves remains uncovered within a former private landholding on the edges of the ancient city.

forte-san-giovanni.name: Fort San Giovanni
forte-san-giovanni.description: Spanish-style fortress built between 1640 and 1645 overlooking Finalborgo, the medieval capital of the Marquisate of Finale, during the period of Spanish rule over the territory. It stands among the best-preserved works of military architecture on the Ligurian coast.

fortezza-di-san-leo.name: Fortress of San Leo
fortezza-di-san-leo.description: Fortress perched on a sheer rock outcrop above San Leo in the Montefeltro, rebuilt in its present form in the fifteenth century for Federico da Montefeltro, likely to a design by Francesco di Giorgio Martini. Under papal rule it served as a prison, most famously holding the adventurer Cagliostro, who died there in 1795.

galleria-borghese.name: Borghese Gallery
galleria-borghese.description: Museum in the Villa Borghese park in Rome, built to display the art collection assembled by Cardinal Scipione Borghese in the early seventeenth century. It holds masterpieces by Bernini, Caravaggio, Titian and Raphael, alongside ancient Roman sculpture.

galleria-giorgio-franchetti-alla-ca-d-or.name: Giorgio Franchetti Gallery at the Ca' d'Oro
galleria-giorgio-franchetti-alla-ca-d-or.description: Gallery inside the Ca' d'Oro, a Gothic palace on the Grand Canal in Venice built in the fifteenth century for the Contarini family and named for the gold leaf that once adorned its facade. Baron Giorgio Franchetti restored the palace in the early twentieth century and bequeathed it to the state along with his art collection, which includes Mantegna's Saint Sebastian.

galleria-spada.name: Spada Gallery
galleria-spada.description: Picture gallery in Palazzo Spada in Rome, assembled mainly by Cardinal Bernardino Spada in the seventeenth century and displayed largely as he arranged it, with works by Titian, Guercino and Guido Reni. The palace courtyard also holds Borromini's celebrated forced-perspective colonnade, which appears to stretch far longer than its actual eight metres.

galleria-dell-accademia-di-firenze.name: Accademia Gallery, Florence
galleria-dell-accademia-di-firenze.description: Museum founded in 1784 as a teaching collection for the adjoining Academy of Fine Arts, now famous above all for housing Michelangelo's David, moved here from Piazza della Signoria in 1873. Its galleries also display the sculptor's unfinished Prisoners and an extensive collection of Florentine Gothic and Renaissance painting.

galleria-nazionale-d-arte-moderna-e-cont.name: National Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art
galleria-nazionale-d-arte-moderna-e-cont.description: Rome's national museum of nineteenth- and twentieth-century art, built in the early 1900s in the Villa Borghese grounds and expanded in the following decades. Its collection ranges from Italian Neoclassical and Futurist works to international modern art, including pieces by Klimt, Cézanne and Van Gogh.

galleria-nazionale-della-puglia-girolamo.name: National Gallery of Puglia "Girolamo and Rosaria Devanna"
galleria-nazionale-della-puglia-girolamo.description: The first national gallery in Puglia, opened in 2009 in the Renaissance-era Palazzo Sylos-Calò in Bitonto, built between 1529 and 1583. Its collection centres on the modern art donated to the Italian state by Girolamo and Rosaria De Vanna.

galleria-nazionale-di-cosenza.name: National Gallery of Cosenza
galleria-nazionale-di-cosenza.description: Museum in Palazzo Arnone, a sixteenth-century building in Cosenza's historic centre that later served as government offices, courthouse and prison before its restoration as a gallery, formally recognised in 2009. Its collections range from paintings by Mattia Preti, Luca Giordano and Jusepe de Ribera to a bronze cast of Boccioni's Unique Forms of Continuity in Space.

gallerie-estensi-galleria-estense.name: Estense Galleries - Estense Gallery
gallerie-estensi-galleria-estense.description: Art gallery in Modena's Palazzo dei Musei, founded in 1854 by Francesco V of Austria-Este and moved to its present home in 1894. Built on the collections of the Este dukes of Ferrara and Modena, depleted when Francesco III sold around a hundred paintings to Augustus III of Poland in 1746 and further reduced by Napoleonic seizures, it holds paintings from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century by Correggio, Velázquez, El Greco and Titian, along with Bernini's marble bust of Francesco I d'Este.

gallerie-estensi-museo-lapidario-estense.name: Estense Galleries - Estense Lapidary Museum
gallerie-estensi-museo-lapidario-estense.description: Museum of stone antiquities in Modena's Palazzo dei Musei, founded in 1828 by Francesco IV d'Este from Este family collections including Alfonso II's Ferrarese antiquities. It holds Roman inscriptions and sarcophagi carved in Ravenna, along with medieval funerary monuments moved here from the city's cathedral and churches.

gallerie-estensi-palazzo-ducale-di-sassu.name: Estense Galleries - Ducal Palace of Sassuolo
gallerie-estensi-palazzo-ducale-di-sassu.description: Baroque residence built from 1634 for Francesco I d'Este on the site of a medieval castle, designed by Bartolomeo Avanzini. Its state rooms are decorated with extensive frescoes led by the French painter Jean Boulanger, including the Galleria di Bacco and the Salone delle Guardie celebrating the Este dynasty.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-cappella-palatina-.name: Uffizi Galleries - Palatine Chapel (Palazzo Pitti)
gallerie-degli-uffizi-cappella-palatina-.description: Court chapel within the Pitti Palace in Florence, part of the Uffizi Galleries, created from a room built under Bartolomeo Ammannati and completed in 1574. It was converted into the grand-ducal chapel from 1766 under Pietro Leopoldo, to a design by the architects Ruggieri and Paoletti, with an altar of 1785 by Santi Pacini and frescoes added in 1791-92 by Luigi Ademollo.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-corridoio-vasarian.name: Uffizi Galleries - Vasari Corridor
gallerie-degli-uffizi-corridoio-vasarian.description: Elevated passageway nearly a kilometre long, built by Giorgio Vasari in 1565 for Cosimo I de' Medici to let the family cross from Palazzo Vecchio to Palazzo Pitti over the Ponte Vecchio without setting foot in the street. Reopened after restoration, it is now hung with a collection of self-portraits.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-galleria-del-costu.name: Uffizi Galleries - Museum of Fashion and Costume (Palazzo Pitti)
gallerie-degli-uffizi-galleria-del-costu.description: Fashion and costume museum opened in 1983 in the Palazzina della Meridiana, a wing of the Pitti Palace in Florence built from 1776 under Grand Duke Pietro Leopoldo to designs by Gaspare Paoletti. Its holdings of more than 6,000 pieces span clothing and accessories from the sixteenth to the twenty-first century, including funerary garments of Cosimo I de' Medici and his family and creations by designers such as Valentino, Armani and Versace.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-galleria-palatina-.name: Uffizi Galleries - Palatine Gallery and State Apartments of Palazzo Pitti
gallerie-degli-uffizi-galleria-palatina-.description: Picture gallery on the first floor of Palazzo Pitti, formed from the Medici and Lorraine grand-ducal collections and still hung in the dense, salon-style arrangement of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It holds major works by Raphael and Titian alongside the adjoining state apartments once used by the palace's ruling families.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-giardino-delle-scu.name: Uffizi Galleries - Garden of the Royal Stables and Pagliere
gallerie-degli-uffizi-giardino-delle-scu.description: Garden of the former royal stables in Florence, part of the Uffizi Galleries and Pitti Palace complex, built between 1866 and 1869 during Florence's period as capital of Italy to house the court's horses and grooms. The green area between the Boboli Garden and Porta Romana includes the stable buildings, now home to the Istituto d'Arte, and the Pagliere hayloft, intended as a museum of twentieth-century figurative art.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-giardino-di-boboli.name: Uffizi Galleries - Boboli Gardens
gallerie-degli-uffizi-giardino-di-boboli.description: Formal garden laid out behind Palazzo Pitti from 1550 for the Medici family, one of the earliest and most influential examples of the Italian garden style. Its terraces, fountains and grottoes, including Buontalenti's Grotta Grande, are populated with statuary spanning antiquity to the twentieth century.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-palazzo-pitti.name: Uffizi Galleries - Palazzo Pitti
gallerie-degli-uffizi-palazzo-pitti.description: Monumental palace begun around 1458 for the Florentine banker Luca Pitti and bought by the Medici in 1549 to become their principal residence. Enlarged over the following two centuries, it now forms a single museum complex with the Palatine Gallery, the Boboli Gardens and several smaller collections.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-tesoro-dei-granduc.name: Uffizi Galleries - Treasury of the Grand Dukes (Palazzo Pitti)
gallerie-degli-uffizi-tesoro-dei-granduc.description: Museum on the ground floor of Palazzo Pitti gathering the precious objects amassed by the Medici and later grand-ducal families, known as the Museo degli Argenti until it was renamed in 2015. Its rooms display goldwork, hardstone vessels, ivories and Oriental porcelain, including the Augsburg cabinet known as the Stipo d'Alemagna.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-galleria-d-arte-mo.name: Uffizi Galleries - Gallery of Modern Art (Palazzo Pitti)
gallerie-degli-uffizi-galleria-d-arte-mo.description: Museum on the second floor of Palazzo Pitti, established in 1924 to trace Italian art from the late-eighteenth-century Neoclassical era to the early twentieth century. Its more than thirty rooms hold a notable group of Macchiaioli paintings by Giovanni Fattori, Silvestro Lega and Telemaco Signorini, many from the Diego Martelli bequest of 1897.

gallerie-degli-uffizi-gli-uffizi.name: Uffizi Galleries - The Uffizi
gallerie-degli-uffizi-gli-uffizi.description: Museum in the office building Vasari designed from 1560 for Cosimo I de' Medici, which became a gallery for the family's art collection and opened to visitors in the sixteenth century, making it one of the oldest museums in the world. Its rooms hold an unrivalled collection of Italian Renaissance painting, including Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera.

gallerie-dell-accademia-di-venezia.name: Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice
gallerie-dell-accademia-di-venezia.description: Museum of Venetian painting housed since 1807 in the former Scuola della Carità on the Grand Canal, originally founded as the gallery of Venice's Academy of Fine Arts. It traces the Venetian school from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century, with major works by Bellini, Giorgione, Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto.

gallerie-nazionali-di-arte-antica-galler.name: National Galleries of Ancient Art - Corsini Gallery
gallerie-nazionali-di-arte-antica-galler.description: Picture gallery in Palazzo Corsini on the Tiber in Rome, built up around the collection of Cardinal Neri Corsini in the eighteenth century and given to the Italian state in 1883. Together with Palazzo Barberini it forms the National Galleries of Ancient Art, and holds works by Caravaggio, Rubens and Fra Angelico.

gallerie-nazionali-di-arte-antica-palazz.name: National Galleries of Ancient Art - Palazzo Barberini
gallerie-nazionali-di-arte-antica-palazz.description: Baroque palace built for Pope Urban VIII by the architect Carlo Maderno, its grand salon crowned by Pietro da Cortona's ceiling fresco, the Allegory of Divine Providence, glorifying the Barberini family. Together with Palazzo Corsini it forms the National Galleries of Ancient Art, and houses paintings by Caravaggio, Raphael's La Fornarina, Titian's Venus and Adonis, Hans Holbein the Younger's portrait of Henry VIII, and works by Guercino.

giardino-della-villa-a-castello.name: Garden of Villa di Castello
giardino-della-villa-a-castello.description: Terraced garden commissioned in 1538 by Duke Cosimo I de' Medici from the architect Niccolò Tribolo, one of the earliest and most influential examples of the Italian garden and a forerunner of the Boboli Gardens. It preserves the Mannerist Grotta degli Animali and citrus collections cultivated since Medici times, and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2013.

giardino-di-villa-il-ventaglio.name: Garden of Villa Il Ventaglio
giardino-di-villa-il-ventaglio.description: Public park in Florence redesigned in the mid-nineteenth century for Count Giuseppe Archinto by the architect Giuseppe Poggi with the botanist Attilio Pucci, who laid out a romantic English-style landscape with a small lake and rose terraces. Acquired by the Italian state in 1969, the villa itself has housed the International University of Art since 1968.

grotta-azzurra.name: Blue Grotto
grotta-azzurra.description: Sea cave on the island of Capri, famed since the nineteenth century for the intense blue light that fills its interior when sunlight passes beneath the water and refracts through the low entrance. Visited by boat, it stands on the site of what is thought to have been a nymphaeum for a Roman-era villa.

grotte-di-catullo-e-museo-archeologico-d.name: Grottoes of Catullus and Archaeological Museum of Sirmione
grotte-di-catullo-e-museo-archeologico-d.description: Ruins of one of the largest Roman residential villas in northern Italy, occupying the tip of the Sirmione peninsula on Lake Garda and traditionally, though without firm proof, linked to the poet Catullus, whose family had property here. The adjoining museum displays finds from the site alongside a model reconstruction of the villa.

ipogeo-dei-volumni-e-necropoli-del-palaz.name: Hypogeum of the Volumni and Necropolis of Palazzone
ipogeo-dei-volumni-e-necropoli-del-palaz.description: Etruscan underground burial chamber near Perugia, built in the second century BCE for the Volumni family and modelled on the layout of a Roman house, with funerary urns still in place around a central figure of the family patriarch. It forms part of the wider Palazzone necropolis excavated along an ancient road leading out of the city.

la-cattolica.name: La Cattolica
la-cattolica.description: Small Byzantine church in Stilo, Calabria, built around the tenth century in brick on a square plan crowned by five domes, one of the finest surviving examples of Byzantine religious architecture in southern Italy. Its interior preserves fragments of medieval fresco decoration.

marrc-museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-re.name: MArRC - National Archaeological Museum of Reggio Calabria
marrc-museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-re.description: Italy's leading museum of Magna Graecia archaeology, gathering material from Greek and indigenous sites across Calabria. It is best known for the Riace Bronzes, two life-size fifth-century BCE Greek warrior statues recovered from the sea off the Calabrian coast in 1972.

mupre-museo-nazionale-della-preistoria-d.name: MUPRE - National Museum of Prehistory of Valle Camonica
mupre-museo-nazionale-della-preistoria-d.description: National prehistory museum in Capo di Ponte, in the historic Villa Agostani, tracing human settlement in Valle Camonica from the Palaeolithic through the Copper Age. It provides context for the valley's UNESCO-listed rock engravings, with exhibits on early habitation, Neolithic land use and prehistoric burial and cult practices.

mausoleo-di-teodorico.name: Mausoleum of Theodoric
mausoleo-di-teodorico.description: Funerary monument built around 520 in Ravenna for Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths, notable for its two-tiered structure and its ten-metre monolithic roof stone, quarried in Istria and lowered into place in a single block. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of Ravenna's early Christian monuments.

monastero-di-san-benedetto-sacro-speco.name: Monastery of San Benedetto - Sacro Speco
monastero-di-san-benedetto-sacro-speco.description: Benedictine monastery near Subiaco, built around the Sacro Speco, the cave where Saint Benedict of Nursia lived as a hermit before founding the Benedictine order; the present Romanesque-Gothic complex was consecrated in the eleventh century. It preserves frescoes ranging from an eighth-century Byzantine-style cycle to a 1223 portrait of Saint Francis of Assisi, regarded as the earliest faithful depiction of the saint, along with a 1657 marble statue of Saint Benedict by Antonio Raggi.

monastero-di-santa-scolastica.name: Monastery of Santa Scolastica
monastero-di-santa-scolastica.description: Benedictine monastery near Subiaco, the only one of the twelve founded by Saint Benedict in the sixth century in this valley still inhabited by monks. Its three cloisters range from a ninth-century core to a Cosmatesque cloister and a Renaissance courtyard, and it houses a historic library and a printing press credited with producing Italy's first printed book, in 1465.

monumenti-e-aree-archeologiche-dell-anti.name: Archaeological Monuments and Areas of Ancient Teate
monumenti-e-aree-archeologiche-dell-anti.description: Group of scattered Roman-era archaeological remains in the historic centre of Chieti, ancient Teate Marrucinorum, chief town of the Marrucini people before the medieval and modern city grew over the site. The remains are managed together with the Museo Nazionale d'Abruzzo as part of Abruzzo's state museum network.

musei-del-bargello-cappelle-medicee.name: Medici Chapels
musei-del-bargello-cappelle-medicee.description: Funerary chapels of the Medici family attached to the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Florence: the Sagrestia Nuova, designed by Michelangelo between 1521 and 1534 with his tombs of Giuliano and Lorenzo de' Medici, and the octagonal Cappella dei Principi, begun in 1604 under Grand Duke Ferdinando I to designs by Matteo Nigetti, its walls faced in inlaid marble and semi-precious stone. A state museum since 1869, it has formed part of the Bargello Museums group since 2014.

musei-del-bargello-chiesa-e-museo-di-ors.name: Church and Museum of Orsanmichele
musei-del-bargello-chiesa-e-museo-di-ors.description: Museum occupying the upper floors of the Orsanmichele loggia in Florence, a former grain market converted into a church whose exterior niches were filled from the 14th century with statues commissioned by the city's guilds. Opened in 1996 to house the original sculptures once the weathered originals outside were replaced by copies, it displays works including Ghiberti's Saint John the Baptist (1412-1416), Donatello's Saint Mark (1411-1413) and Verrocchio's Incredulity of Saint Thomas (1467-1483).

musei-del-bargello-museo-nazionale-del-b.name: Bargello Museums - National Museum of the Bargello
musei-del-bargello-museo-nazionale-del-b.description: Museum in Florence's oldest public building, begun in 1255 as the seat of the chief magistrate and later used as a prison before opening as a sculpture museum in 1865. Its collection is centred on Renaissance sculpture, with key works by Donatello, Verrocchio and a young Michelangelo.

musei-e-parchi-archeologici-di-praeneste.name: National Archaeological Museum of Palestrina
musei-e-parchi-archeologici-di-praeneste.description: Archaeological museum in Palestrina, founded in 1956 and set on the upper terraces of the ancient Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia within Palazzo Colonna Barberini. It displays finds from ancient Praeneste, including funerary goods from the local necropoleis and the Nile Mosaic, a 2nd-century-BC depiction of the river from Ethiopia to the Mediterranean thought to be the work of Alexandrian craftsmen.

musei-e-parchi-archeologici-di-melfi-e-v.name: "Massimo Pallottino" National Archaeological Museum of the Melfese
musei-e-parchi-archeologici-di-melfi-e-v.description: Archaeological museum in the Castle of Melfi, inaugurated in 1976 and dedicated to archaeologist Massimo Pallottino. It preserves finds from the Vulture-Melfese area spanning prehistory to the Norman period, including the 2nd-century-AD Roman sarcophagus of Rapolla, and, since a 2021 reopening in the castle's Marcangione Tower, Swabian and Angevin ceramics and glassware.

musei-e-parchi-archeologici-di-melfi-e-v.name: "Mario Torelli" National Archaeological Museum of Venosa
musei-e-parchi-archeologici-di-melfi-e-v.description: Archaeological museum in Venosa, housed in the Aragonese Castello Pirro del Balzo, inaugurated in 1991 and renamed in 2021 after archaeologist Mario Torelli. Its five sections present finds from the prehistoric site of Notarchirico and from ancient Venusia, spanning the pre-Roman period to the 9th century AD.

musei-nazionali-di-ferrara-pinacoteca-na.name: National Museums of Ferrara - National Picture Gallery of Ferrara
musei-nazionali-di-ferrara-pinacoteca-na.description: Picture gallery in Palazzo dei Diamanti, Ferrara, dedicated to the local school of painting that flourished at the Este court in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Its collection includes works by Cosmè Tura, Ercole de' Roberti and Garofalo, drawn largely from churches and convents suppressed after the unification of Italy.

musei-nazionali-di-genova-galleria-nazio.name: National Museums of Genoa - National Gallery of Palazzo Spinola
musei-nazionali-di-genova-galleria-nazio.description: Museum in Palazzo Spinola di Pellicceria, a late-sixteenth-century Genoese palace built for Francesco Grimaldi and later owned by the Spinola family, who donated it to the Italian state in 1958. Kept largely in its original furnished state, it holds paintings by Antonello da Messina, Van Dyck and Luca Cambiaso, and is part of the UNESCO-listed Palazzi dei Rolli.

musei-nazionali-di-genova-palazzo-reale-.name: Royal Palace of Genoa
musei-nazionali-di-genova-palazzo-reale-.description: Baroque palace in Genoa built between 1643 and 1650 for the Balbi family and later enlarged by the Durazzo family, whose Hall of Mirrors, designed by Carlo Fontana and decorated by Domenico Parodi, is its best-known interior; it passed to the House of Savoy in 1824 and to the Italian state in 1919. Now a museum, it displays more than 200 paintings, including works by Van Dyck, Tintoretto and Luca Giordano, and is part of the UNESCO-listed Strade Nuove and the System of the Palazzi dei Rolli.

musei-nazionali-di-matera-ex-ospedale-sa.name: National Museums of Matera - Former Hospital of San Rocco
musei-nazionali-di-matera-ex-ospedale-sa.description: Former hospital building beside the church of Cristo Flagellato in Matera, transferred to the city's national museum in 2022 as an exhibition venue. It now forms part of the network of sites through which the Museo Nazionale di Matera presents the city's art and history.

musei-nazionali-di-matera-museo-domenico.name: Domenico Ridola National Archaeological Museum
musei-nazionali-di-matera-museo-domenico.description: Archaeological museum in Matera, the oldest in Basilicata, founded in 1911 when senator and physician Domenico Ridola donated his archaeological collections to the state. Housed in the former convent of Santa Chiara, it displays material from the Paleolithic to the 3rd century BC, including Neolithic Serra d'Alto pottery and red-figure vases by the Pisticci Painter.

musei-nazionali-di-matera-palazzo-lanfra.name: Palazzo Lanfranchi
musei-nazionali-di-matera-palazzo-lanfra.description: Museum of medieval and modern art in Matera, opened in 2003 in the 17th-century Palazzo Lanfranchi. Its collections range from medieval and 18th-century Neapolitan sacred art to forty-four paintings by Carlo Levi, including the large canvas Lucania '61, shown at the 1961 Italia '61 exhibition in Turin.

musei-nazionali-di-perugia-galleria-nazi.name: National Museums of Perugia - National Gallery of Umbria
musei-nazionali-di-perugia-galleria-nazi.description: Umbria's principal art museum, occupying the upper floors of the Palazzo dei Priori in Perugia and tracing the region's painting from the thirteenth to the nineteenth century. Its collection is especially strong in works by Perugino, along with Piero della Francesca, Pinturicchio and Fra Angelico.

musei-nazionali-di-siena-museo-archeolog.name: National Museums of Siena - National Archaeological Museum of Siena
musei-nazionali-di-siena-museo-archeolog.description: Archaeological museum founded in 1933 by Ranuccio Bianchi Bandinelli, now housed in the former hospital complex of Santa Maria della Scala on Piazza del Duomo. Its collection, drawn from excavations across Siena province, includes Etruscan red-figure pottery, Roman sarcophagi and alabaster funerary urns.

musei-nazionali-di-siena-palazzo-chigi-a.name: Palazzo Chigi alla Postierla
musei-nazionali-di-siena-palazzo-chigi-a.description: Renaissance palace in Siena overlooking Piazza di Postierla, built in the second half of the 16th century, possibly to a design by Bartolomeo Neroni known as il Riccio, on a site named after a gate in the city's earlier walls. Two of its halls preserve original decoration, with frescoes and canvases by the Flemish painter Bernard van Rantwyck and 1573 stuccowork by Marcello Sparti of Urbino.

musei-nazionali-di-siena-villa-brandi.name: Villa Brandi
musei-nazionali-di-siena-villa-brandi.description: 16th-century country villa at Vignano, near Siena, acquired by the Brandi family in the 18th century and later the home of art historian and restoration theorist Cesare Brandi, who bequeathed it to the Italian state. It preserves his personal art collection, with works by Morandi, Guttuso, Burri and De Pisis, together with his library and archive of letters and photographs.

musei-reali-di-torino.name: Royal Museums of Turin
musei-reali-di-torino.description: Complex of museums in Turin uniting the former residences and collections of the House of Savoy, including the Royal Palace, the Royal Armoury, the Sabauda Gallery and the Museum of Antiquities, set around the Royal Gardens. Together they present the dynasty's paintings, arms and archaeological holdings built up over centuries of Savoy rule.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-altamura.name: National Archaeological Museum of Altamura
museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-altamura.description: Museum opened in 1997 in Altamura, presenting the ancient settlement of the High Murgia plateau through prehistoric, archaic, classical-Hellenistic and medieval sections. It is closely tied to the nearby La Croce site and to the discovery of the Altamura Man, a fossilised Neanderthal skeleton found in a local cave.

museo-diego-aragona-pignatelli-cortes.name: Diego Aragona Pignatelli Cortes Museum
museo-diego-aragona-pignatelli-cortes.description: Neoclassical villa in Naples built in the early nineteenth century and later home to the Pignatelli Cortes family, who left it to the Italian state along with its furnishings and art collection. Its rooms preserve period decoration and porcelain, and the grounds include a carriage museum.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-mantova.name: National Archaeological Museum of Mantua
museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-mantova.description: National archaeological museum of Mantua, occupying the late-19th-century Mercato dei Bozzoli, a former silk-cocoon market built on the site of the Gonzaga court theatre and given to the state with its original wooden roof trusses preserved. Its collection spans the Neolithic through the Renaissance and includes the 'Lovers of Valdaro,' a pair of Neolithic skeletons found embraced in a 2007 excavation and on display since 2011.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-muro-luc.name: National Archaeological Museum of Muro Lucano
museo-archeologico-nazionale-di-muro-luc.description: National archaeological museum dedicated to north-western Lucania, inaugurated in 2008 after five years of restoration of the 16th-century Palazzo del Seminario, itself repaired following the 1980 Irpinia earthquake. Its five sections, drawing on excavations begun in 1980, cover the Peuketiantes and Lucanian peoples, Romanization and Roman villas of the area.

museo-giacomo-manzu.name: Giacomo Manzù Museum
museo-giacomo-manzu.description: Museum in Ardea dedicated to the sculptor Giacomo Manzù, who lived and worked nearby and chose the site for his burial. Opened in 1981 as the first Italian museum devoted to a living artist, it houses around 460 works he donated in 1979, including bronze sculptures and drawings such as studies for his cathedral doors in Salzburg and Rotterdam.

museo-nazionale-d-abruzzo-forte-spagnolo.name: National Museum of Abruzzo - Spanish Fort
museo-nazionale-d-abruzzo-forte-spagnolo.description: State museum of archaeology and art in L'Aquila, housed in the 16th-century Forte Spagnolo, a fortress overlooking the city. Opened in 1951, its collections range from the mounted skeleton of a prehistoric southern mammoth found in 1954 to medieval and Renaissance sculpture by artists such as Silvestro dell'Aquila; the fort, damaged by the 2009 earthquake, reopened to the public after restoration.

museo-archeologico-dell-abbazia-greca-di.name: Archaeological Museum of the Greek Abbey of San Nilo
museo-archeologico-dell-abbazia-greca-di.description: Small archaeological museum inside the Abbey of San Nilo (Abbazia di Grottaferrata), an Italo-Byzantine Basilian monastery near Rome founded in 1004 by Nilus of Rossano and fortified in the early 16th century for Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II. The museum displays archaeological finds recovered in the surrounding area.

museo-archeologico-dell-agro-falisco-e-f.name: Archaeological Museum of the Ager Faliscus and Forte Sangallo
museo-archeologico-dell-agro-falisco-e-f.description: Archaeological museum housed within Forte Sangallo, a fortress built around 1500 for Pope Alexander VI in Civita Castellana, on the site of the ancient Faliscan capital of Falerii Veteres. The collection documents the pre-Roman Faliscan civilisation, with painted pottery, terracotta votives and material from local necropoleis.

museo-archeologico-della-penisola-sorren.name: Georges Vallet Territorial Archaeological Museum of the Sorrento Peninsula
museo-archeologico-della-penisola-sorren.description: Archaeological museum in Piano di Sorrento, opened in 1999 inside the eighteenth-century Villa Fondi De Sangro and named after the French archaeologist Georges Vallet, a specialist in the Greek colonies of Magna Graecia. It presents finds documenting the ancient settlement of the Sorrento peninsula.

museo-archeologico-di-metauros.name: Archaeological Museum of Metauros
museo-archeologico-di-metauros.description: Museum near Gioia Tauro preserving finds from Metauros, a Greek colony founded in the seventh century BCE by settlers from Zancle, which traded across the Mediterranean before declining after epidemics and medieval invasions. Its collection, drawn mainly from the site's necropolis, includes Attic black-figure pottery and imported ceramics documenting the city's trade links.

museo-archeologico-di-santa-maria-delle-.name: Archaeological Museum of Santa Maria delle Monache
museo-archeologico-di-santa-maria-delle-.description: National Palaeolithic museum in Isernia, housed in the former monastic complex of Santa Maria delle Monache, dedicated to the nearby Isernia La Pineta site discovered in 1978. The exhibition displays stone tools, animal remains and a reconstruction of the prehistoric landscape from one of Europe's most important early human sites, where a hominin milk tooth dated to around 583,000 years ago was found.

museo-archeologico-di-vulci.name: National Archaeological Museum of Vulci
museo-archeologico-di-vulci.description: State archaeology museum housed in the Castello dell'Abbadia, a former 12th-century Benedictine abbey remodeled in the early 16th century under Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, the future Pope Paul III, and overlooking an Etruscan-Roman bridge over the Fiora river. Established in 1975, it presents finds from the Etruscan and Roman city of Vulci, largely drawn from excavations of its necropolises carried out from the 19th century onward.

museo-archeologico-lametino.name: Lametino Archaeological Museum
museo-archeologico-lametino.description: Archaeological museum in Lamezia Terme preserving finds from the surrounding territory, including material from the ancient Greek city of Terina. Its holdings include Terinaean coins and Greek pottery recovered from local excavations.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-vito-capial.name: Vito Capialbi National Archaeological Museum
museo-archeologico-nazionale-vito-capial.description: Archaeological museum inside the Norman-Swabian castle of Vibo Valentia, built on what is thought to have been the acropolis of the ancient Greek city of Hipponion, founded in the seventh century BCE by colonists from Locri. Its collection spans Greek votive pottery from the sanctuary of Scrimbia to Roman-era material from the later city of Vibo.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-concordiese.name: National Concordiese Museum of Portogruaro
museo-archeologico-nazionale-concordiese.description: Archaeological museum in Portogruaro, among the oldest in the Veneto region, dedicated to finds from the Roman city of Iulia Concordia, the ancient settlement now known as Concordia Sagittaria. Its collection documents the town's role as a road junction and military outpost through inscriptions, sculpture and everyday objects recovered in the area.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-la-civitell.name: National Archaeological Museum "La Civitella" of Chieti
museo-archeologico-nazionale-la-civitell.description: National archaeological museum opened in 2000 following the 1982 discovery of a Roman amphitheatre, designed by architect Ettore De Lellis as a partly underground structure integrated with the La Civitella archaeological park. Tracing its origins to the 1938 Antiquarium Teatinum, it presents finds from ancient Teate and the Marrucini people alongside material from the wider Pescara valley spanning prehistory to the Middle Ages.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-d-abruzzo-v.name: National Archaeological Museum of Abruzzo - Villa Frigerj
museo-archeologico-nazionale-d-abruzzo-v.description: National archaeological museum of the Abruzzo region, opened in 1959 in Villa Frigerj, a neoclassical villa built around 1830 for Baron Ferrante Frigerj by architect Enrico Riccio. Its collection traces Abruzzo from prehistory to the late Roman period, including the Warrior of Capestrano statue and a numismatic collection of around 15,000 coins.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-agro-a.name: National Archaeological Museum of the Agro Atellano
museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-agro-a.description: National archaeological museum covering the Agro Atellano, the southern part of ancient Campania, established in 1991 and opened to the public in 2002. Its three-floor display spans the Bronze Age to late antiquity, with Campanian red-figure pottery, amphora burials of infants, and orientalizing-period grave goods from Gricignano di Aversa.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-alta-v.name: National Archaeological Museum of the Alta Val d'Agri - Grumento Nova
museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-alta-v.description: National archaeological museum established in the late 20th century beside the Grumentum archaeological park in the Alta Val d'Agri. Displays span the Bronze Age to the early Middle Ages, with material from the indigenous Oenotrian and Magna Graecia cultures alongside finds from the Roman city of Grumentum, presented across two floors with panels reconstructing the city's monuments.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-umbria.name: National Archaeological Museum of Umbria
museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-umbria.description: National archaeological museum of the Umbria region, established in 1948 around collections dating back to 1790, and housed in the former Dominican convent of San Domenico in Perugia. Its holdings trace regional prehistory through the Roman period, including the Etruscan Cippus of Perugia, bronzes from Castel San Mariano and a reconstructed Etruscan tomb.

museo-archeologico-nazionale-dell-antica.name: National Archaeological Museum of Ancient Allifae
