parco-archeologico-di-pompei-scavi-arche.description: Roman patrician villa at Stabiae, on the hillside above modern Castellammare di Stabia, buried along with Pompeii and Herculaneum in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. Excavated from the 18th century onward, it preserves peristyles and richly frescoed rooms, including a wall painting of Ariadne that gave the villa its modern name.

parco-archeologico-di-pompei-scavi-arche.name: Villa San Marco
parco-archeologico-di-pompei-scavi-arche.description: Roman patrician villa at Stabiae, near modern Castellammare di Stabia, one of the largest seaside residences excavated on the Bay of Naples before it was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. It is arranged around a large colonnaded peristyle and swimming pool, with rooms decorated in fresco, and takes its modern name from a nearby church of San Marco.

parco-archeologico-di-pompei-scavi-di-op.name: Oplontis
parco-archeologico-di-pompei-scavi-di-op.description: Roman suburban site at Torre Annunziata, buried in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. Its centrepiece is the Villa of Poppaea, a luxurious 1st-century-BC residence later enlarged, decorated with mythological frescoes of Hercules and Apollo and traditionally linked to Poppaea Sabina, wife of Nero, on the basis of a painted inscription found on an amphora. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997, together with Pompeii and Herculaneum.

parco-archeologico-di-pompei-villa-regin.name: Pompeii Archaeological Park - Villa Regina
parco-archeologico-di-pompei-villa-regin.description: Roman villa rustica at Boscoreale, part of the wider Pompeii Archaeological Park, buried like Pompeii itself by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE. Excavated from the late 1970s, it preserves a wine-making complex with buried dolia and a press, and its vineyard has been replanted with ancient vine varieties to produce wine again.

parco-archeologico-di-roselle.name: Roselle Archaeological Park
parco-archeologico-di-roselle.description: Archaeological park north of Grosseto preserving the Etruscan and Roman city of Roselle, settled from the early 7th century BCE on hills overlooking the former Lake Prile. Its walls, over three kilometres long and dating to the 6th century BCE, are among the best-preserved Etruscan fortifications; the city, conquered by Rome in 294 BCE, remained a bishopric until its diocese was transferred to Grosseto in 1138.

parco-archeologico-di-sepino-area-archeo.name: Sepino Archaeological Park - Altilia-Saepinum Archaeological Area
parco-archeologico-di-sepino-area-archeo.description: Archaeological park 3 km north of modern Sepino in Molise, preserving the Samnite vicus and later Roman municipium of Saepinum. Its 1,270-metre perimeter wall with four monumental gates encloses a forum, basilica, macellum, baths and a well-preserved theatre, largely brought to light in excavations directed by Valerio Cianfarani in the 1950s.

parco-archeologico-di-sepino-museo-della.name: Sepino Archaeological Park - Museum of the City and Territory
parco-archeologico-di-sepino-museo-della.description: Archaeological park in Molise preserving the Roman town of Saepinum in the Altilia hamlet, with its city walls, basilica, forum and theatre laid out in the Tammaro valley. The adjoining Museum of the City and Territory occupies 18th-century rural buildings raised directly over the Roman theatre's curved structure and displays finds from prehistoric to medieval times found on the site and in the surrounding area.

parco-archeologico-di-siponto.name: Siponto Archaeological Park
parco-archeologico-di-siponto.description: Archaeological park at Manfredonia preserving the remains of ancient Siponto, a Roman colony from 194 BCE and later an important episcopal seat, including a 4th-century early Christian basilica with a mosaic floor, underground burial chambers and city walls. Since 2016 the ruined basilica's lost volumes have been evoked by a wire-mesh installation created by artist Edoardo Tresoldi.

parco-archeologico-di-vetulonia.name: Vetulonia Archaeological Park
parco-archeologico-di-vetulonia.description: Archaeological park at the site of Vetulonia, one of the twelve cities of the Etruscan League in northern Etruria, occupied from the Iron Age into the Roman period. Physician Isidoro Falchi identified the site and led excavations from 1884 to 1913, uncovering rich orientalizing tombs such as the Tomba del Duce and the Tomba della Pietrera, alongside the later Poggiarello Renzetti residential quarter with its Hellenistic-Roman houses and paved streets.

parco-archeologico-nazionale-dei-massi-d.name: Massi di Cemmo National Archaeological Park
parco-archeologico-nazionale-dei-massi-d.description: National archaeological park at Capo di Ponte in Val Camonica protecting two large boulders bearing the valley's earliest documented rock carvings, first recorded in 1909 by geographer Gualtiero Laeng. Engraved with animals, weapons and daily-life scenes during the Copper Age, the rocks stand within a small sanctuary area that was expanded and formally inaugurated as a national park in 2005.

parco-archeologico-urbano-dell-antica-vo.name: Urban Archaeological Park of Ancient Volcei
parco-archeologico-urbano-dell-antica-vo.description: Urban archaeological park running beneath and around the historic centre of Buccino, on the site of the ancient Lucanian and Roman town of Volcei, whose walls date to the 4th century BCE. Opened in 2003 following extensive excavations carried out after the 1980 earthquake, the park's underground and elevated walkways reveal mosaics, roads and shops layered beneath the medieval and modern town.

parco-archeologico-urbano-dell-antica-pi.name: Urban Archaeological Park of Ancient Picentia
parco-archeologico-urbano-dell-antica-pi.description: Urban archaeological park in Pontecagnano Faiano preserving part of ancient Picentia, a Roman colony founded in 268 BCE over an earlier pre-Roman settlement. Excavated areas reveal street grids and residential blocks in use from the 4th to the 3rd century BCE, when the town was abandoned; the park is managed as a green space alongside its ongoing role as an excavation site for the universities of Salerno and Molise.

parco-delle-tombe-di-virgilio-e-leopardi.name: Park of the Tombs of Virgil and Leopardi
parco-delle-tombe-di-virgilio-e-leopardi.description: Park in the Piedigrotta district of Naples, laid out around a Roman-era columbarium traditionally venerated since antiquity as the tomb of the poet Virgil. Since 1939 it has also held the tomb of Giacomo Leopardi, moved here from the church of San Vitale a Fuorigrotta, and it opens onto the entrance of the Crypta Neapolitana, a Roman tunnel linking Piedigrotta to Fuorigrotta.

parco-delle-incisioni-rupestri-con-rupe-.name: Rock Engravings Park with the Rupe Magna of Grosio
parco-delle-incisioni-rupestri-con-rupe-.description: Park in Valtellina protecting the Rupe Magna, the largest engraved alpine rock face known, discovered in 1966 by archaeologist Davide Pace on land above the town of Grosio. Its surface bears more than 5,000 carvings of human and animal figures, geometric motifs and everyday objects made between the late Neolithic and the Iron Age; the park was established in 1978 after the surrounding land, including a ruined castle, was donated to the state.

parco-nazionale-delle-incisioni-rupestri.name: National Park of Rock Engravings
parco-nazionale-delle-incisioni-rupestri.description: Established in 1955 at Naquane near Capo di Ponte, this was the first archaeological park created in Italy and, in 1979, became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage site. Spread over 14 hectares, it displays 104 engraved rocks among the more than 300,000 figures carved across Val Camonica by the ancient Camunni people from around 8000 BCE through the Roman period.

pinacoteca-di-brera.name: Brera Picture Gallery
pinacoteca-di-brera.description: Milan's principal public picture gallery, opened in 1809 within the Palazzo di Brera on the initiative of Napoleon, who gathered works confiscated from churches and religious orders across northern Italy to form its core collection. Its holdings centre on Italian painting from the 14th to the 20th century, including major works by Raphael, Mantegna, Piero della Francesca and Caravaggio.

pinacoteca-nazionale-di-bologna.name: National Picture Gallery of Bologna
pinacoteca-nazionale-di-bologna.description: Bologna's principal picture gallery, formed from paintings gathered from suppressed churches and monasteries after the Napoleonic confiscations of the late 18th century and now housed beside the city's Academy of Fine Arts. Its collection traces the Bolognese school from the Middle Ages through the Baroque, with major works by Vitale da Bologna, Francesco Francia and the Carracci family.

pinacoteca-nazionale-di-cagliari.name: National Picture Gallery of Cagliari
pinacoteca-nazionale-di-cagliari.description: Picture gallery in Cagliari's Cittadella dei Musei complex, built between 1956 and 1979 within the city's former royal arsenal. Its core collection formed after the 1875 demolition of the church of San Francesco brought a large group of Catalan and local Gothic retables into state hands, later joined by Sardinian, Italian, Spanish and Flemish paintings from the 15th century onward and 19th-century ethnographic pieces.

pinacoteca-nazionale-di-sassari.name: National Picture Gallery of Sassari
pinacoteca-nazionale-di-sassari.description: Picture gallery in Sassari's former Jesuit Collegio Canopoleno, opened to the public in 2008 to display around 400 paintings from the Middle Ages to the 20th century. Its holdings derive largely from private collections donated to the city in the late 19th century, notably by the entrepreneur Giovanni Antonio Sanna in 1875.

pinacoteca-nazionale-e-museo-di-palazzo-.name: National Picture Gallery and Museum of Palazzo Mansi
pinacoteca-nazionale-e-museo-di-palazzo-.description: National picture gallery and period residence in Lucca, occupying a palazzo built at the end of the 17th century for the Mansi family and acquired by the state in 1965. Alongside 16th- to 18th-century Italian and foreign paintings, the museum preserves original furnishings and a cycle of Brussels tapestries in the family's historic apartments.

reggia-di-caserta-palazzo-reale.name: Royal Palace of Caserta
reggia-di-caserta-palazzo-reale.description: Vast royal palace built from 1752 for Charles of Bourbon, King of Naples, to designs by architect Luigi Vanvitelli, intended to rival Versailles as the seat of the new Bourbon capital. Its 1,200 rooms and monumental staircase surround a park with cascading fountains and an English garden, and the complex was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1997.

residenze-reali-sabaude-complesso-monume.name: Savoy Royal Residences - Ducal Castle, Garden and Park of Agliè
residenze-reali-sabaude-complesso-monume.description: Component of the UNESCO-listed Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, the castle at Agliè grew from a 12th-century fortress of the San Martino counts into a Baroque residence after Amedeo di Castellamonte's 1667 remodelling. Acquired by the Savoy family in 1764 and passed to the Italian state in 1939, it preserves frescoed apartments, a gallery of knights' portraits, and a romantic park landscaped in the 1830s-40s by the German gardener Xavier Kurten.

residenze-reali-sabaude-complesso-monume.name: Savoy Royal Residences - Monumental Complex of Racconigi Castle and Park
residenze-reali-sabaude-complesso-monume.description: Savoy royal residence south of Turin with origins as an 11th-century fortified manor, later a possession of the Marquises of Saluzzo before passing to the House of Savoy in the second half of the 14th century. Remodelled from 1676 by architect Guarino Guarini and repeatedly enlarged, it served as a summer retreat for the Savoy-Carignano branch and the kings of Sardinia and Italy; the state acquired it in 1980, and it was inscribed with the other Savoy residences on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997.

residenze-reali-sabaude-palazzo-carignan.name: Savoy Royal Residences - Palazzo Carignano
residenze-reali-sabaude-palazzo-carignan.description: Baroque palace in central Turin designed by Guarino Guarini and built in 1679-1685 as the residence of the Princes of Carignano, part of the UNESCO-listed Residences of the Royal House of Savoy. Birthplace of King Victor Emmanuel II, it housed the Subalpine Chamber of Deputies from 1848 and the first Italian Parliament from 1861, and today its piano nobile hosts the Museo Nazionale del Risorgimento Italiano.

residenze-reali-sabaude-villa-della-regi.name: Savoy Royal Residences - Villa della Regina
residenze-reali-sabaude-villa-della-regi.description: Hillside villa above Turin, part of the UNESCO-listed Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, begun around 1615 to a design by Ascanio Vitozzi for Cardinal Maurizio of Savoy and completed by Carlo and Amedeo di Castellamonte. Later remodelled by Filippo Juvarra for Queen Anna Maria of Orléans, it retains a terraced Italian garden with the Neptune fountain of the Gran Rondeau and a hillside vineyard that again produces Freisa di Chieri wine.

resti-della-citta-romana-di-mevaniola.name: Remains of the Roman Town of Mevaniola
resti-della-citta-romana-di-mevaniola.description: Archaeological area near Galeata preserving the remains of Mevaniola, a town of Umbrian origin later enlarged under Roman rule and mentioned by Pliny the Elder, abandoned around the 4th-5th century CE. Excavations along the old road descending the Bidente valley have uncovered a bath complex with mosaic floors and a cistern.

rocca-albornoz-museo-nazionale-del-ducat.name: Rocca Albornoz - National Museum of the Duchy of Spoleto
rocca-albornoz-museo-nazionale-del-ducat.description: Hilltop fortress overlooking Spoleto, built from 1359 on the orders of Cardinal Egidio Albornoz to designs by Matteo di Giovannello, known as Gattapone, as part of a network of strongholds restoring papal authority over central Italy. Used from 1816 as a prison, it now houses the National Museum of the Duchy of Spoleto, opened in 2007, which traces the history of the Lombard duchy from the 4th to the 15th century.

rocca-roveresca-di-senigallia.name: Rovere Fortress of Senigallia
rocca-roveresca-di-senigallia.description: Renaissance fortress built between 1476 and 1482 for Giovanni della Rovere, lord of Senigallia and nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, with the residential wing designed by Luciano Laurana and the defensive works completed by Baccio Pontelli. In 1503 it was the setting for the massacre of rival condottieri by Cesare Borgia, an episode later recounted by Niccolò Machiavelli.

rocca-di-gradara.name: Gradara Castle
rocca-di-gradara.description: Medieval fortress built around 1150 by the De Grifo family and later held by the Malatesta, Sforza and Della Rovere lords, whose successive rebuildings shaped the castle and the walled village around it. Tradition, though undocumented, places within its walls the tragic love affair of Paolo and Francesca, killed by Francesca's husband Gianciotto Malatesta in 1289 and immortalised by Dante in the Divine Comedy.

santuario-madonna-della-quercia.name: Sanctuary of the Madonna della Quercia
santuario-madonna-della-quercia.description: Marian sanctuary at Bagnaia, near Viterbo, built between 1470 and 1525 around a venerated image of the Virgin said to have been placed on an oak tree in 1417 and to have become an object of pilgrimage during the plague of 1467. Consecrated in 1578 and elevated to the rank of minor basilica in 1867, the church displays glazed terracotta lunettes attributed to the workshop of Andrea della Robbia above its three portals.

santuario-di-minerva-di-breno.name: Sanctuary of Minerva at Breno
santuario-di-minerva-di-breno.description: Sanctuary in Val Camonica where an earlier place of worship, in use from the 5th century BCE, was replaced in the early 1st century CE by a Roman temple dedicated to Minerva, enlarged under the Flavian emperors when the valley gained the status of an independent Roman community. Its main hall held a marble statue of the goddess copying a 5th-century-BCE Greek original; the sanctuary fell out of use by the late 4th century CE and was rediscovered only in 1986, opening to visitors in 2007.

santuario-italico.name: Italic Sanctuary of Pietrabbondante
santuario-italico.description: The most important religious and political centre of the Samnite Pentri people, built on an artificial terrace on the slopes of Monte Saraceno between the 2nd century BCE and 95 BCE. Its theatre-temple complex, an entirely Italic architectural conception combining a theatre with a temple dedicated to deities such as Honos and Virtus, reflects the wealth and vitality of the Samnite world before the Social War.

santuario-preistorico-di-monte-d-accoddi.name: Prehistoric Sanctuary of Monte d'Accoddi
santuario-preistorico-di-monte-d-accoddi.description: Prehistoric sanctuary near Sassari centred on a monumental stepped altar shaped like a truncated pyramid, built with a 42-metre ramp during the early Copper Age, around 3500-2900 BCE. Excavations directed by Ercole Contu from the 1950s and later by Santo Tiné revealed beneath it an earlier structure known as the Red Temple, dated to the Ozieri culture of the late Neolithic; the monument has no known parallel in prehistoric Europe and is often compared to Mesopotamian ziggurats.

sede-espositiva-in-palazzo-ducale-di-tri.name: Exhibition Venue at the Ducal Palace of Tricarico
sede-espositiva-in-palazzo-ducale-di-tri.description: Exhibition space in the Ducal Palace of Tricarico, a hill town in Basilicata's Matera province that was long the seat of the local feudal lordship. The venue hosts displays related to the town's history and territory within the historic palace building.

teatro-romano-di-benevento.name: Roman Theatre of Benevento
teatro-romano-di-benevento.description: Roman theatre built in the late 1st or early 2nd century CE, probably under Trajan, and inaugurated by the emperor Hadrian in 126 CE according to a dedicatory inscription; a second inscription indicates further work completed under Caracalla. With a diameter of around 90 metres, it could seat up to 15,000 spectators and remains one of the largest Roman theatres in southern Italy.

teatro-romano-di-sarno.name: Roman Theatre of Sarno
teatro-romano-di-sarno.description: Archaeological remains of a Roman-period theatre in the town of Sarno, in Campania's Sarno river valley, an area that saw dense settlement in antiquity. The remains attest to the urban development achieved by the ancient settlement during the Roman era.

tempietto-sul-clitunno.name: Clitunno Tempietto
tempietto-sul-clitunno.description: Small church near the springs of the river Clitunno, built in the form of a Corinthian temple and now dated on stylistic grounds to the Lombard period, between the early 7th and 8th centuries. Dedicated to San Salvatore, it was long mistaken for an actual Roman temple, even by the 16th-century architect Palladio, and was inscribed in 2011 as part of the UNESCO serial site 'Longobards in Italy: Places of Power'.

tempio-delle-tavole-palatine.name: Temple of the Tavole Palatine
tempio-delle-tavole-palatine.description: Doric temple dedicated to Hera, built in the 6th century BCE in an extraurban sanctuary near Metaponto that marked the border between the Greek colony's territory and that of rival Taranto. Of an original peristyle of 32 columns, 15 survive standing, making it, alongside the temples of Paestum, one of the best-preserved examples of Greek architecture in southern Italy.

terme-taurine-o-di-traiano.name: Taurine Baths (Baths of Trajan)
terme-taurine-o-di-traiano.description: Roman bath complex north of Civitavecchia, begun in the Sullan era of the early 1st century BCE and greatly enlarged under Trajan and again under Hadrian, remaining in use until the late 5th century CE. Its name, recorded by the poet Rutilius Namatianus in 416 CE, derives from a legend in which a bull scraped the earth to reveal the hot sulphurous springs feeding the baths.

terme-di-caracalla.name: Baths of Caracalla
terme-di-caracalla.description: Vast public baths in Rome, inaugurated in 216 CE under the emperor Caracalla and remaining in use until the Ostrogothic siege severed the city's aqueducts in the 6th century. Covering some 25 hectares, the complex could accommodate over a thousand bathers at once and its towering brick ruins, once lined with marble, mosaics and statuary, illustrate the scale of Roman imperial architecture.

tomba-di-cicerone.name: Tomb of Cicero
tomba-di-cicerone.description: Augustan-age funerary tower along the Appian Way at Formia, traditionally known as the Tomb of Cicero, who was killed near the town in 43 BCE on the orders of Mark Antony after mentioning his villa there, the Formianum, in his letters. The attribution to the orator is a long-standing local tradition rather than an established fact, since no inscription or archaeological evidence confirms it.

torre-di-cicerone.name: Tower of Cicero
torre-di-cicerone.description: Medieval tower of the 11th-12th century standing on the acropolis of Arpino, the birthplace of Marcus Tullius Cicero in 106 BCE, and known by local tradition as the Tower of Cicero. Standing 30 metres high within the town's Cyclopean walls, it takes its name from an oral tradition linking the site to the orator's family property, though no residential remains confirming the connection have been found.

villa-adriana-e-villa-d-este-area-archeo.name: Hadrian's Villa Archaeological Area
villa-adriana-e-villa-d-este-area-archeo.description: The vast villa complex built from around 118 CE as a retreat for the emperor Hadrian near Tivoli, combining palace buildings, baths, theatres and gardens laid out around structures inspired by monuments the emperor had seen on his travels, including reproductions evoking Egypt and Greece. One of the largest and most lavish residences of the Roman world, it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1999.

villa-adriana-e-villa-d-este-santuario-d.name: Sanctuary of Hercules Victor
villa-adriana-e-villa-d-este-santuario-d.description: One of the largest sanctuaries of Republican Italy, built on a monumental terrace above Tivoli between the late 2nd and early 1st century BCE and dedicated to Hercules Victor, protector of the nearby wool trade and of travellers on the Via Tiburtina. Its ruins later served as the foundation for paper mills that operated on the site into the 20th century, layering industrial archaeology over the ancient sanctuary.

villa-adriana-e-villa-d-este-villa-d-est.name: Villa d'Este
villa-adriana-e-villa-d-este-villa-d-est.description: Renaissance villa and garden at Tivoli, created from 1550 for Cardinal Ippolito II d'Este, governor of Tivoli and son of Lucrezia Borgia, who converted a former Benedictine convent into a residence celebrated for its terraced garden of fountains fed by the waters of the Aniene river. Its elaborate hydraulic system, including the Organ Fountain and the Avenue of a Hundred Fountains, made it a model for European garden design and led to its inscription as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2001.

villa-damecuta.name: Villa Damecuta
villa-damecuta.description: Ruins of one of the twelve villas that, according to Suetonius, the emperor Tiberius had built on Capri, constructed on a promontory near the Blue Grotto between around 27 and 36 CE. Its most striking surviving feature is an 80-metre porticoed loggia that opened onto the Bay of Naples and ended in a semicircular belvedere; a medieval watchtower was later raised on the site.

villa-floridiana.name: Villa Floridiana
villa-floridiana.description: Neapolitan villa and park acquired in 1815 by King Ferdinand IV of Bourbon for his morganatic wife, Lucia Migliaccio, Duchess of Floridia, and remodelled in neoclassical style by architect Antonio Niccolini with a romantic garden laid out by Friedrich Dehnhardt. Purchased by the state in 1919, it has housed the Duca di Martina ceramics museum since 1927, built around a collection of decorative arts assembled by the duke and donated by his niece.

villa-lante-bagnaia.name: Villa Lante at Bagnaia
villa-lante-bagnaia.description: Renaissance villa and garden at Bagnaia, near Viterbo, built between 1511 and 1566 for Cardinal Gianfrancesco Gambara to a design by Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola, comprising two matching pavilions flanking a formal garden fed by an elaborate water chain. Regarded as one of the finest examples of an Italian Renaissance garden, it passed after the cardinal's death in 1587 to his nephew and later to the Lante family, from whom it takes its name.

villa-pisani-stra-venezia.name: Villa Pisani, Stra (Venice)
villa-pisani-stra-venezia.description: Grand villa on the Brenta canal near Venice, built from 1721 for the Pisani family to designs by Gerolamo Frigimelica and Francesco Maria Preti and eventually comprising more than a hundred rooms. Purchased by Napoleon in 1807 and given to his stepson Eugène de Beauharnais, it later became an Austrian imperial residence; its ballroom ceiling bears Giambattista Tiepolo's 1761 fresco 'Apotheosis of the Pisani Family', and its park contains a celebrated boxwood maze.

villa-romana-e-antiquarium.name: Roman Villa and Antiquarium of Desenzano del Garda
villa-romana-e-antiquarium.description: Roman villa on Lake Garda at Desenzano, built from the late 1st century BCE and substantially rebuilt in the 4th century CE into a luxurious residence with polychrome floor mosaics depicting hunting and harvest scenes. Discovered by chance in 1921 during house-building work, the site is now paired with an Antiquarium museum, inaugurated in 1971, that displays finds from the excavations.

villa-romana-e-antiquarium-di-palazzo-pi.name: Roman Villa and Antiquarium of Palazzo Pignano
villa-romana-e-antiquarium-di-palazzo-pi.description: Roman villa on the plain near Crema, dated to the late Roman period (4th-5th century CE), with mosaic-floored rooms and an unusual circular building of debated function, possibly linked to a bath suite or an early Christian use. An adjoining antiquarium displays finds recovered from the site.

villa-rosa-museo-dell-arte-vetraria-alta.name: Villa Rosa - Museum of Altare Glass Art
villa-rosa-museo-dell-arte-vetraria-alta.description: Museum dedicated to the historic glassmaking tradition of Altare, a Ligurian town whose glassworkers' guild dates back to the Middle Ages and long rivaled Murano as a center of European glass production. Housed in the Villa Rosa, it displays glass objects and tools documenting the craft's techniques and history.

villa-del-colle-del-cardinale.name: Villa del Colle del Cardinale
villa-del-colle-del-cardinale.description: Country residence near Perugia built from around 1575 for Cardinal Fulvio della Corgna, nephew of Pope Julius III, likely to a design by architect Galeazzo Alessi, combining a working farm estate with a summer retreat. Its main hall preserves a coffered wooden ceiling and frescoes signed in 1581 by Salvio Savini, with further decoration added in the 18th century; the villa passed through several noble families before the Italian state acquired it in 1996.

villa-di-livia.name: Villa of Livia
villa-di-livia.description: Roman villa at Prima Porta, on the Via Flaminia north of Rome, identified as a residence of Livia, wife of the emperor Augustus, and excavated from 1863-1864. The dig brought to light the celebrated marble statue of Augustus of Prima Porta, now in the Vatican Museums, and a subterranean hall painted around 30-20 BCE with one of the earliest and finest examples of continuous Roman garden fresco, detached in 1951 and now displayed in Rome's Palazzo Massimo.

villa-di-orazio.name: Villa of Horace
villa-di-orazio.description: Roman villa in the Sabine hills at Licenza, identified with the country estate given to the poet Horace by his patron Maecenas around 33-32 BCE, which the poet celebrated in his verse as a peaceful refuge from Rome. The site, pinpointed in the 17th century by the scholar Lucas Holstenius, preserves a large porticoed garden and mosaic floors, and finds are displayed in the adjoining Museo Oraziano.

villa-medicea-della-petraia.name: Medici Villa of Petraia
villa-medicea-della-petraia.description: Medici villa on the hills above Florence, acquired in 1568 by Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici and transformed around a medieval castle tower into a country residence, with a courtyard later covered by a glass roof and decorated with frescoes celebrating the Medici dynasty. Its formal Italian garden, with terraces, fountains and a large fishpond, survives largely intact, and the villa was inscribed with the other Medici residences on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2013.

villa-medicea-di-cerreto-guidi-e-museo-s.name: Medici Villa of Cerreto Guidi and Museum of Hunting and Territory History
villa-medicea-di-cerreto-guidi-e-museo-s.description: Hunting lodge built for Grand Duke Cosimo I de' Medici between 1564 and 1567 on the site of a former Guidi counts' fortress, with distinctive symmetrical zigzag ramps attributed to Bernardo Buontalenti. Isabella de' Medici was murdered here in 1576 by her husband; recognized since 2013 as part of the UNESCO-listed Medici Villas and Gardens, it has housed the Museo storico della caccia e del territorio since 2002.

villa-medicea-di-poggio-a-caiano-e-giard.name: Medici Villa of Poggio a Caiano and Garden
villa-medicea-di-poggio-a-caiano-e-giard.description: Medici villa built from 1485 for Lorenzo the Magnificent to a design by architect Giuliano da Sangallo, considered the prototype of the Renaissance villa with its raised loggia and temple-like portico. Its salon preserves frescoes by Andrea del Sarto, Pontormo and Franciabigio celebrating the Medici family, and the villa was inscribed with Florence's other Medici residences and gardens on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2013.

villa-romana-del-varignano.name: Roman Villa of Varignano
villa-romana-del-varignano.description: Roman villa near Portovenere, developed from the late 2nd century BCE and substantially rebuilt during the Sullan era of the early 1st century BCE as the centre of an agricultural estate specialising in olive oil production. Excavated between 1967 and 1986, it preserves what is regarded as the oldest olive press in Liguria alongside a residential wing with private baths, and remained in use until around the 6th century CE.

villa-romana-di-russi.name: Roman Villa of Russi
villa-romana-di-russi.description: Roman rustic villa near Ravenna, active during the 1st and 2nd centuries CE as an agricultural estate supplying provisions to the imperial fleet based at nearby Classe, before declining after the fleet's personnel were transferred to Constantinople in 330 CE. Discovered in 1938 and excavated from the 1950s, the 8,000-square-metre complex preserves geometric floor mosaics that rank it among the best-preserved Roman villas in northern Italy.

vittoriano-e-palazzo-venezia-museo-centr.name: Vittoriano and Palazzo Venezia - Central Museum of the Risorgimento of Rome
vittoriano-e-palazzo-venezia-museo-centr.description: National museum devoted to the Italian Risorgimento, housed within the Vittoriano monument in central Rome and dedicated to the movements and events that led to Italian unification in the 19th century. Its collections of documents, uniforms, weapons, paintings and memorabilia trace the period from the late 18th century through the First World War.

vittoriano-e-palazzo-venezia-museo-nazio.name: Vittoriano and Palazzo Venezia - National Museum of Palazzo Venezia
vittoriano-e-palazzo-venezia-museo-nazio.description: National museum in Palazzo Venezia, one of Rome's earliest Renaissance palaces, built from 1455 for the Venetian cardinal Pietro Barbo, later Pope Paul II, and used in the 20th century as Benito Mussolini's official office. Its collections range across medieval and Renaissance sculpture, decorative arts, tapestries and paintings, including bronzes and ceramics from the papal and Farnese periods of the building's history.

vittoriano-e-palazzo-venezia-vittoriano.name: Vittoriano and Palazzo Venezia - The Vittoriano
vittoriano-e-palazzo-venezia-vittoriano.description: Monumental white marble complex in the centre of Rome, built to honour King Victor Emmanuel II, first king of a unified Italy, to a design by architect Giuseppe Sacconi selected in an international competition and inaugurated in 1911. It incorporates the Altare della Patria and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, added after the First World War, and now also hosts museum exhibitions and a panoramic terrace.
